1. Large Language Model Foundations
A large language model is a neural network trained to predict tokens from context. During
training, the model receives enormous collections of text and learns statistical patterns involving
words, grammar, style, facts, and common reasoning structures. The model does not store a
conventional database of complete sentences. Instead, information is distributed across many
numerical parameters that influence which token is likely to come next.
When a user sends a prompt, the text is converted into tokens and passed through multiple
transformer blocks. Each block updates the internal representation of every token by considering
relationships with other tokens. The final layer produces a probability distribution over the model
vocabulary. A decoding strategy chooses the next token, appends it to the sequence, and
repeats the process until the answer finishes or reaches a configured limit.
Language models are strong at generating fluent text, summarizing documents, classifying
content, extracting structured information, and transforming text between formats. They are not
guaranteed truth engines. The

Key ideas include tokens, context, parameters, decoding, and uncertainty. A model can provide
a useful answer without having a human-style understanding of the subject. The application

2. Tokens, Context, and Embeddings
A tokenizer divides text into smaller units called tokens. A token may represent a complete word,
part of a word, punctuation, or whitespace. Tokenization allows a model to work with a finite
vocabulary while still handling unfamiliar words. Context windows, usage limits, latency, and API
costs are commonly measured in tokens rather than characters or words.
The context window contains all information available to the model for the current generation. It
may include a system instruction, conversation history, the current user message, retrieved
passages, and tool results. Information outside the context window is not directly visible to the
model. Applications often shorten older conversations, summarize history, or retrieve only
relevant documents.
An embedding converts text into a numerical vector. Texts with similar meanings tend to produce
vectors located near each other in vector space. Embeddings are useful for semantic search
because they can match meaning rather than exact keywords. A question about annual leave
can retrieve a document about vacation days even if the two texts use differ

ngs are useful for semantic search
because they can match meaning rather than exact keywords. A question about annual leave
can retrieve a document about vacation days even if the two texts use different wording.
A retrieval system should use the same embedding model for documents and queries. Changing
the model without rebuilding the index can make stored vectors incompatible with new query
vectors. Metadata such as document name, page number, section, version, and access level
should be stored beside every vector.

3. Transformer Blocks and Attention
The transformer is the core architecture behind most modern language models. A model
contains many repeated transformer blocks. Each block normally includes self-attention, a
feed-forward network, normalization, and residual connections. Repeating these operations
allows the model to build increasingly useful representations of the input sequence.
Self-attention helps each token identify other relevant tokens. For every token, the model
calculates query, key, and value vectors. Queries are compared with keys to produce attention
weights, and those weights control how values are combined. Multi-head attention performs this
process in parallel, allowing different heads to focus on different relationships.
Decoder-only language models use a causal mask. This prevents a token from attending to
future tokens during generation. When predicting the next token, the model can use the prompt
and all tokens already generated, but it cannot see tokens that have not yet been produced. This
design matches the next-token prediction objective used during training.

Residual connections add the original input back after a transformation, which helps information
and gradients travel through deep networks. Layer normalization stabilizes values. The
feed-forward network transforms each token representation independently after attention has
mixed contextual information.

4. Prompt Design and Conversation Roles
A prompt communicates the task, relevant context, constraints, and expected output. Clear
prompts describe what the model should do, identify the audience, specify the required format,
and explain what to do when information is unavailable. Ambiguous prompts force the model to
infer missing requirements and usually create less predictable results.
Chat applications commonly organize input into system, user, and assistant roles. The system
message defines broad behavior and boundaries. User messages contain requests and data.
Assistant messages preserve previous responses so the model can continue the conversation.
These roles are serialized into tokens before inference.
Zero-shot prompting gives instructions without examples. One-shot prompting provides one
example, while few-shot prompting provides several examples. Examples are useful when the
output format, classification labels, tone, or decision criteria are difficult to describe. They should
be accurate, diverse, and consistent with the instructions.

Prompt quality can be tested systematically. Keep a fixed evaluation set, change one prompt
element at a time, and compare accuracy, format compliance, latency, and token usage. A
prompt that performs well on one example may fail on unusual wording, missing information,
adversarial text, or long documents.

5. Hallucination and Answer Reliability
A hallucination is an unsupported or incorrect model statement presented as if it were reliable.
Hallucinations occur because language models optimize next-token prediction rather than factual
verification. When evidence is missing, a model may continue a plausible linguistic pattern
instead of stopping. Fluent language can make an incorrect answer appear convincing.
Common causes include missing knowledge, outdated training data, ambiguous questions,
conflicting context, high sampling randomness, and pressure to always provide an answer. In
retrieval systems, poor document selection is another major cause. If the correct passage is not
retrieved, the generation model cannot reliably use it.
Applications can reduce hallucination by supplying trustworthy context, lowering temperature for
factual tasks, requesting citations, validating structured output, and allowing the model to state
that information is unavailable. Critical decisions require deterministic business rules or human
review rather than relying only on generated language.

mation is unavailable. Critical decisions require deterministic business rules or human
review rather than relying only on generated language.
Evaluation should separate retrieval quality from generation quality. Retrieval metrics determine
whether the right evidence was found. Faithfulness checks determine whether the answer is
supported by that evidence. Answer relevance determines whether the response addresses the
question.

6. Retrieval-Augmented Generation Overview
Retrieval-augmented generation, usually called RAG, connects a language model to an external
knowledge source. Instead of expecting the model to remember every fact, the application
searches a document collection for relevant passages and places those passages in the prompt.
The model then generates an answer using the retrieved evidence.
A RAG system has two broad phases. The indexing phase loads documents, extracts text,
cleans it, divides it into chunks, creates embeddings, and stores the resulting vectors with
metadata. The query phase embeds the user question, retrieves similar chunks, optionally
reranks them, constructs a prompt, and asks the language model to answer.
RAG can make answers more current, domain-specific, and traceable. Updating the knowledge
base is often easier than retraining a language model. It also allows answers to include
references to source documents. However, RAG does not automatically guarantee correctness.
Poor parsing, weak chunking, incomplete metadata, or irrelevant retrieval can still produce bad
answers.

AG does not automatically guarantee correctness.
Poor parsing, weak chunking, incomplete metadata, or irrelevant retrieval can still produce bad
answers.
Successful RAG projects treat ingestion and retrieval as data engineering problems. They define
document ownership, update schedules, versioning, quality checks, access controls,
observability, and recovery procedures. A polished chatbot interface cannot compensate for an
unreliable knowledge pipeline.

7. Document Ingestion and Cleaning
Document ingestion begins by collecting source files and recording where they came from.
Sources may include PDFs, web pages, office documents, database rows, support tickets, or
APIs. Each source should receive a stable identifier and metadata describing its owner, creation
time, version, permissions, and processing status.
Text extraction is not always straightforward. Digital PDFs usually contain selectable text, while
scanned PDFs contain images and require optical character recognition. Tables may lose their
rows and columns during extraction. Headers, footers, page numbers, navigation elements, and
repeated legal notices can pollute the content and reduce retrieval quality.
Cleaning should preserve meaning while removing noise. Useful steps include normalizing
whitespace, repairing broken line endings, removing repeated headers, identifying headings,
retaining page references, and detecting empty or corrupted pages. Every transformation should
be reproducible so the index can be rebuilt when processing rules change.
Data quality checks can measure extraction success, text length, language,

pty or corrupted pages. Every transformation should
be reproducible so the index can be rebuilt when processing rules change.
Data quality checks can measure extraction success, text length, language, duplicate content,
missing pages, and unusual character ratios. Failed documents should be quarantined for review
rather than silently entering the vector index. Logging each stage makes it possible to diagnose
why a later answer used incomplete evidence.

8. Chunking Strategies
Chunking divides long documents into smaller pieces that can be embedded and retrieved.
Chunk size creates a tradeoff. Very small chunks may lose context and produce vague matches.
Very large chunks may contain several unrelated topics, waste context-window space, and
reduce retrieval precision.
Fixed-size chunking splits text after a chosen number of characters or tokens. It is simple and
fast but may cut sentences or sections at awkward points. Overlap repeats part of one chunk in
the next chunk, reducing the chance that important information is separated at a boundary.
Excessive overlap increases storage and creates nearly duplicate search results.
Structure-aware chunking respects headings, paragraphs, lists, or document sections. Semantic
chunking attempts to detect topic changes using embeddings or language models. These
methods can preserve meaning better but require more processing and careful testing. The best
strategy depends on document structure and user questions.
Each chunk should store metadata such as document identifier, page number, section title,
chunk sequence, source version, and permis

The best
strategy depends on document structure and user questions.
Each chunk should store metadata such as document identifier, page number, section title,
chunk sequence, source version, and permissions. Chunking should be evaluated with real
questions. If answers require information from several distant sections, the system may need
parent-child retrieval, neighboring chunks, or query decomposition.

9. Vector Search and Similarity
After chunking, an embedding model converts each chunk into a vector. These vectors are
stored in a vector index or vector database. At query time, the same embedding model converts
the question into a vector. The system then searches for document vectors that are close to the
query vector.
Cosine similarity compares the direction of two vectors and is widely used for semantic search.
Other indexes may use dot product or Euclidean distance. The database can use approximate
nearest-neighbor algorithms to search millions of vectors quickly. Approximation improves speed
while accepting a small possibility of missing the exact nearest result.
Semantic similarity alone may not be sufficient. Metadata filters can restrict results to a
department, customer, date range, language, or permission level. Hybrid retrieval combines
embeddings with keyword search, helping with exact product names, codes, identifiers, and rare
terminology. Reranking uses another model to reorder candidate passages.

Retrieval parameters include the number of candidates, similarity threshold, filters, and reranking
depth. Increasing the number of chunks can improve recall but may add irrelevant context. These
settings should be tuned using representative questions and known relevant passages rather

10. Building the Generation Prompt
After retrieval, the application combines instructions, retrieved passages, conversation history,
and the current question. The prompt should clearly separate trusted application instructions
from untrusted document text. Retrieved content may contain irrelevant statements or malicious
instructions, so the model should treat it as evidence rather than authority.
A grounded prompt tells the model to answer from the supplied context, identify uncertainty, and
avoid unsupported claims. It may require citations containing document names and page
numbers. The application should generate citations from stored metadata instead of trusting the
model to invent source details.
Context ordering can influence results. Highly relevant passages are often placed near the
question or presented with clear labels. Duplicate chunks should be removed to preserve space.
If retrieved evidence conflicts, the prompt can ask the model to describe the conflict instead of
selecting a version without explanation.

Conversation history must be managed carefully. A follow-up question may depend on earlier
turns, but unlimited history increases tokens and can distract retrieval. Applications commonly
rewrite the latest question into a standalone search query, summarize older dialogue, or retain
only turns relevant to the current topic.

11. Evaluation, Security, and Operations
RAG evaluation should include a dataset of realistic questions, expected evidence, and
acceptable answers. Retrieval can be measured with recall at k, precision, and ranking metrics.
Generated answers can be evaluated for relevance, faithfulness, completeness, citation
accuracy, tone, and format compliance. Human review remains important.
Latency is another key measurement. Time to first token captures perceived responsiveness,
while end-to-end latency measures the complete request. Retrieval time, reranking time, model
generation time, and queue time should be recorded separately. Percentiles such as p50, p95,
and p99 reveal slow experiences that averages can hide.
Prompt injection occurs when user content or retrieved documents attempt to override
application instructions. Defenses include treating external text as untrusted, limiting tool
permissions, validating tool arguments, requiring confirmation for consequential actions, filtering
inaccessible documents, and keeping secrets outside prompts.
Operational systems need logging, monitoring, version control, and feedback loops. Teams

Operational systems need logging, monitoring, version control, and feedback loops. Teams
should track which model, embedding model, prompt, index version, and documents produced
each answer. This lineage makes failures reproducible. A mature RAG system is a governed
